articles.title: Astro MD vs MDX: Content Collection Build Performance
articles.excerpt: Standard Markdown (.md) and MDX (.mdx) process content drastically differently within Astro content collections. The build pipeline parses standard Markdown as raw text data, requiring minimal memory…
articles.body: Standard Markdown ( .md ) and MDX ( .mdx ) process content drastically differently within Astro content collections. The build pipeline parses standard Markdown as raw text data, requiring minimal memory and scaling linearly. The build process compiles MDX files into full JSX components, forcing the Vite bundler to process every .mdx file as a discrete JavaScript module. This architectural difference means MDX processing introduces significant parser overhead and increases build times on low-resource homelab CI runners. Use standard Markdown for static text and reserve MDX strictly for files requiring embedded interactive components. Astro Markdown vs MDX: Parser Architecture Standard .md files in Astro bypass the JavaScript module graph entirely.

articles.title: Where the Beam Actually Lands: Coverage from Beam Angle and Mounting Height
articles.excerpt: A datasheet gives you a beam angle and a mounting height. What you actually need to know is how much floor the radar covers, and how much of that footprint is usable. Those are two different questions…
articles.body: A datasheet gives you a beam angle and a mounting height. What you actually need to know is how much floor the radar covers, and how much of that footprint is usable. Those are two different questions, and the published figures answer them separately. This article works the geometry out for the three modules we ship, using published beam angles and published mounting heights. It also deals with the gap that appears when you put the two published numbers next to each other — the geometric footprint and the quoted detection range often do not agree, and when they disagree, one of them is the harder bound. Two quantities, not one Quantity Set by Nature Geometric footprint Beam angle and mounting height Geometry. Calculable, and a hard bound.

articles.title: From Franka Arms to Humanoids: 11 LeRobot v3.0 Datasets for VLA Training in 2026
articles.excerpt: A field guide to 11 robot-learning datasets, from Franka arms to full humanoids and real teleoperation to simulation, reformatted into LeRobotDataset v3.0 and loaded into FiftyOne with their exact fie…
articles.body: A field guide to 11 robot-learning datasets, from Franka arms to full humanoids and real teleoperation to simulation, reformatted into LeRobotDataset v3.0 and loaded into FiftyOne with their exact fields and per-frame streams. A vision-language-action (VLA) model doesn't learn from a folder of images. It learns from episodes: a camera stream, a robot's joint state, and the action it took, all stamped to the same clock and lined up frame by frame. Get that alignment wrong, and the model can't tell which arm motion caused which visual change. The training signal disappears. This makes data engineering a prerequisite for modeling. We pulled together 11 datasets in LeRobot v3.0 , from a Franka arm to a Unitree G1 humanoid and a fully synthetic manipulation suite.

articles.title: Isolate Shared State Before Adding Parallel Test Workers
articles.excerpt: Parallel test runs break on shared state, not CPU count. Here is how we isolated databases, temp files, locks, and reports in a Symfony coverage run, locked only the truly shared fixtures, and merged…
articles.body: Parallel test runs break on shared state, not CPU count. Here is how we isolated databases, temp files, locks, and reports in a Symfony coverage run, locked only the truly shared fixtures, and merged coverage without hiding failures. TLDR Parallel test failures usually come from shared state, not too few CPUs. Give each process its own database suffix, and each queued test its own TMPDIR, lock store, JUnit file, and coverage file. Lock only the fixtures that must stay shared, and keep those locks outside the per-test TMPDIR. Warm one-time installs first, build the queue from phpunit --list-tests, and merge coverage with phpcov after the run. Let the test exit code win, and treat any test that passes only on rerun as a bug report.

articles.title: What If Your AI Code Reviewer Remembered Bugs That Haven’t Happened Yet!
articles.excerpt: Your tests are green. Your AI reviewer approves the pull request. The change ships. Three hours later, a customer gets charged twice. The bug wasn’t hidden in a complicated algorithm. It lived in an a…
articles.body: Your tests are green. Your AI reviewer approves the pull request. The change ships. Three hours later, a customer gets charged twice. The bug wasn’t hidden in a complicated algorithm. It lived in an assumption nobody wrote down: “This operation must happen before that one.” What if your AI code reviewer could discover that assumption, deliberately break it in a sandbox, and remember the resulting failure—before a customer ever experienced it? That’s the idea behind the Counterfactual Wiki. Not a record of what went wrong. A memory of what could go wrong, backed by executable evidence. The missing layer between documentation and testing Documentation describes how a system is supposed to work. Tests check selected behaviors. Incident reports explain how the system actually failed.
articles.author: Seyed Alireza Alhosseini

articles.title: How to Learn Vim (and Actually Remember the Commands)
articles.excerpt: Most people who try Vim quit in the same week. They run vimtutor, get through it in half an hour, feel pretty good, and then open a real file on Monday and can't remember how to delete a word. So they…
articles.body: Most people who try Vim quit in the same week. They run vimtutor , get through it in half an hour, feel pretty good, and then open a real file on Monday and can't remember how to delete a word. So they reach for the arrow keys, then the mouse, then VS Code. I don't think the problem is Vim being hard. It's that people learn the commands once and never see them again until they need them under pressure. If you're searching "how to learn Vim," you'll find cheat sheets with 150 commands on them. Skip those for now. This post is about learning a small set well enough that your fingers know it, and then growing it slowly. Start with vimtutor, but only once vimtutor ships with Vim. Type it in a terminal and you get a plain text lesson you edit as you go.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 28, 1971: Britain launches its 1st satellite Prospero into space on a Black Arrow rocket
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 28, 1971, the United Kingdom launched its first satellite. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 28, 1971, the United Kingdom launched its first satellite. The satellite was named Prospero, but it was also known as the X-3. This wasn't Britain's first satellite , but it was the first and only one the British space program launched with one of its own rockets. The first six British satellites all launched from the United States on NASA rockets. Prospero launched on a carrier rocket called the Black Arrow. The Prospero mission was the fourth and final flight of a Black Arrow rocket . Prospero was designed to study how the environment in space affects communications satellites. It tested things solar cells and telemetry systems, and even had a micrometeoroid detector that would determine small particles in space posed a threat to the spacecraft.

articles.title: 5 days beneath the waves: What it's like to live in an underwater 'space station'
articles.excerpt: Confined inside a research station 22 feet (7 meters) underwater, Analog Astronaut Commander Dr. Musilova and her crew performed research and maintenance activities like future astronauts on Mars.
articles.body: Living underwater was surprisingly peaceful. It was in many ways exactly what I imagine living on Mars would be like one day. There were no humans around us, except for my three SEA STAR crewmembers and me. Apart from the human noises we made, we couldn't hear anything other than the life support systems keeping us alive submerged 22 feet (7 meters) below the surface. We were living in these extreme conditions to study the challenges astronauts may face on long-duration space missions. Since performing research in space is still rare and expensive, there are numerous facilities around the world that focus on recreating space-like conditions on Earth . One of those stations is the Jules' Undersea Lab, where the SEA STAR simulated space mission took place.

articles.excerpt: Joshua Kutryk will venture outside the International Space Station on Oct. 29, on the first spacewalk by a Canadian astronaut in more than seven years. Here's how to watch it live.
articles.body: The next International Space Station (ISS) spacewalk will have more maple-leaf flavor than usual, as a Canadian astronaut will become the first to go outside the orbiting complex in seven years. Canadian Space Agency (CSA) astronaut Joshua Kutryk, who's also a colonel in the Royal Canadian Air Force, will help the ISS boost its power supply during his first-ever spacewalk on Thursday (Oct. 29). Kutryk will be joined by NASA astronaut Anil Menon, who has done three spacewalks already and also serves as a colonel with the U.S. Space Force . The duo are scheduled to venture outside the orbiting lab at 8 a.m. EDT (1200 GMT), kicking off a spacewalk that will last roughly 6 hours and 45 minutes. You can watch it live here at Space.com , courtesy of NASA, beginning at 6:30 a.m. EDT (1030 GMT).

articles.body: Rep. Greg Landsman (D-OH) wants to bring back the federal EV tax credit and double it. His new bill, the “21st Century Vehicle Choice Act” (H.R. 10881), would offer up to $15,000 on a new electric vehicle and $8,000 on a used one, and it would make both credits permanent. The problem is that the bill has virtually no chance of becoming law anytime soon. And if EV shoppers start holding out for it, it could end up hurting the market it’s trying to help. more…

articles.title: Meet Apeiron, Virgin Galactic's 1st 'Delta-class' space plane
articles.excerpt: Virgin Galactic has officially unveiled its first "Delta-class" space plane, and announced the results of the worldwide vote to choose its name.
articles.body: Virgin Galactic has officially unveiled the first space plane in its next-gen "Delta" line, and announced the results of the worldwide vote to choose its name. Spaceship Apeiron will be the first Delta-class vehicle, Virgin Galactic revealed on Wednesday (Oct. 28). Apeiron (pronounced "A'-per-on," according to the announcement) takes its name from the ancient Greek word meaning "boundless," and was selected through a public poll that drew votes from thousands of people across 83 countries and six continents. The reveal comes on the same day that the space plane is scheduled to be flown from its manufacturing facility in Mesa, Arizona, to Spaceport America in New Mexico, where the vehicle will undergo final preparations before beginning flight tests.
